case_study_insert.main_stem: Fleetline Logistics Express (FLE) is a private limited company in the courier and parcel-delivery sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2014 by Sofia Marin, the business delivers parcels for online retailers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. FLE plans to invest $560,000 in a fleet of electric delivery vans, financed by a $360,000 five-year bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.50 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently delivers 52,000 units a year. FLE faces two operational problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and parcel mis-sorts are rising, creating complaints from retailers about damaged or late items.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The depot sorted 13,400 parcels last month with a mis-sort rate of 2.9%, down from 4.6% a year before. Customer complaints fell from 61 to 33 per month. Average delivery time is 1.9 days. A survey of 400 online retailers found that 68% would pay up to $0.30 more for carbon-neutral delivery, and 55% rank delivery speed as their top criterion. A training needs analysis shows 12 of 40 couriers lack electric-van handling skills; on-the-job training is available at the depot, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $620 per courier.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Fleetline Logistics Express for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.00 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills across the courier sector. (3) Electricity and fuel input costs rose 11.2% year-on-year, e-commerce parcel volumes grew 7.4%, and consumer spending fell 1.2% as households tightened budgets.

questions.question_text: FLE plans to fund its $560,000 electric van fleet with a $360,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for FLE of using this bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $360,000 bank loan gives FLE the full capital immediately, allowing all 40 couriers to switch to electric vans at once rather than waiting to accumulate $200,000 of retained profit. Spread over five years, repayments are predictable and can be matched to the $9.00 selling price and 52,000-parcel volume, so the fleet can start reducing the 2.9% mis-sort rate without delay.

Point 2: Using the loan leaves FLE's $200,000 retained profit free as a cash buffer for the 11.2% rise in electricity and fuel costs and for the $620 per courier training bill. Sofia Marin also keeps full ownership and control of the private limited company, since the lender has no equity claim, and the loan can be serviced from the gross profit shown in Appendix 2 without diluting future returns or surrendering a share of the growing parcel business. With revenue of $1,800,000 in 2024 shown in Appendix 2, the $360,000 facility is comfortably within FLE's capacity to service.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to FLE and its van-fleet financing decision.

questions.question_text: FLE is promoting its carbon-neutral electric-van delivery service. Consider a national television campaign, local newspaper advertising, or partnerships with online retailers. Which should FLE choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV campaign would build fast, wide awareness of carbon-neutral delivery among all households, but airtime and production costs are very high and most viewers never choose a courier. For a 40-employee firm servicing a $360,000 loan and facing 11.2% higher fuel and electricity costs, the spend wastage would be severe.

Local newspaper advertising: Regional press is far cheaper and can target specific catchment areas, carrying a simple reliability message to local readers. Its limitation is narrow reach and an ageing readership; the 68% of 400 surveyed retailers willing to pay $0.30 more for carbon-neutral delivery are commercial buyers spread across the country, not local newspaper readers.

Partnerships with online retailers: Working directly with the retailers FLE already serves puts the carbon-neutral message in front of the exact decision-makers, with the $0.30 premium embedded at checkout and measurable sales data. The 55% of surveyed retailers who rank delivery speed first can be shown that electric vans protect reliability, and partnership costs are far lower than TV.

Recommendation: FLE should choose partnerships with online retailers. This reaches the precise segment in the survey, costs little and reinforces speed and reliability at the point of sale. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with a $360,000 loan; local newspapers are rejected as too narrow and poorly matched to commercial buyers, though a small local press test could support the partnership campaign. The 1.9-day average delivery time can be demonstrated in retailer-facing material to support the message.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of FLE with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of FLE with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspapers are rejected.

questions.question_text: FLE's labour turnover has reached 14% and it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for FLE of democratic leadership in reducing courier labour turnover.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives FLE's workforce of 40 a genuine say in how the electric-van fleet is introduced, satisfying social and esteem needs and raising job satisfaction. Couriers who help shape delivery rounds and charging schedules are more likely to stay, directly reducing the 14% labour turnover that currently forces repeated recruitment and disrupts the 52,000-parcel operation.

Point 2: Involving couriers surfaces practical ideas for cutting the 2.9% mis-sort rate, because they handle the parcels every day. Higher involvement builds commitment to Sofia Marin's business, reduces the $620 per courier replacement training cost and protects service quality as the $560,000 van fleet arrives. Loyal couriers also sustain the delivery speed that 55% of surveyed retailers rank as their top criterion, protecting FLE's retailer contracts. The mis-sort rate has already fallen from 4.6% to 2.9%, showing that involved couriers can improve quality, which democratic leadership reinforces. Retaining experienced couriers also protects the 1.9-day delivery time that retailers value.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FLE's labour turnover, quality and output.

questions.question_text: FLE must train 12 couriers to handle the new electric vans. Consider on-the-job training at the depot or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should FLE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training with the actual vans at the depot is directly relevant to FLE's routes and charging routines, costs no course fees, and keeps the 12 couriers productive while they learn, protecting the 52,000-parcel operation and the drive to cut the 2.9% mis-sort rate. However, trainers are working couriers whose own deliveries suffer, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no formal certificate, which may matter if retailers audit service standards.

Off-the-job training: A college course at $620 per courier gives structured electrical-vehicle knowledge and a recognised certificate for all 12, costing $7,440 in total — small against the $560,000 fleet investment. It takes couriers off the road, reducing short-term capacity, and generic content may not match FLE's exact routes, so depot follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: FLE should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, supported by short college sessions for senior couriers. It is cheapest, vehicle-specific and avoids further capacity loss while labour turnover is already 14%; full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $7,440 and releasing 12 couriers would damage the delivery schedule retailers depend on, and college modules can be added once the fleet is running smoothly. With 13,400 parcels sorted last month, removing 12 couriers even briefly would slow the depot while complaints still run at 33 a month. On-the-job training keeps the 52,000-parcel target on track, and the $7,440 saved could fund short college modules later if electric-vehicle knowledge proves insufficient. Senior couriers can later train the remaining staff, so the depot keeps its 1.9-day delivery promise while the fleet expands.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to FLE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of FLE.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of FLE with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how FLE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($9.00 − $4.50) = $180,000 ÷ $4.50 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.00 − $4.50 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways FLE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 52,000 units gives a margin of safety of 12,000 units, confirming the parcel operation is profitable and supporting the $560,000 electric-van investment.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.50 lets managers model the $0.30 premium from the retailer survey: if used as a discount instead, contribution would fall to $4.20 and break-even would rise to about 42,857 units ($180,000 ÷ $4.20), so extra volume must be won.
3. With fixed costs of $180,000, managers can calculate the parcel volume needed to service the $360,000 loan and check that 52,000 units covers it before taking on more debt.
4. Unit cost data ($180,000 ÷ 52,000 units + $4.50 = $7.96 a unit) can be tracked monthly to spot the rising 2.9% mis-sort rate and to judge whether the 11.2% electricity and fuel rise is being absorbed without cutting the $4.50 contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 12,000 units against 52,000 output; discount modelling with $0.30 and $4.20 contribution; loan servicing against $180,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.96 to tackle mis-sorts.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate the profitability of FLE by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has FLE's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $720,000 on revenue of $1,800,000 compares with 2025 gross profit of $945,000 on revenue of $2,100,000; cost of sales rose only from $1,080,000 to $1,155,000 while revenue grew faster. Operating profit increased from $216,000 to $294,000, and capital employed from $1,200,000 to $1,400,000; interest payable rose from $24,000 to $35,000 but stays modest.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The 40.0% to 45.0% movement means FLE retained more of each revenue dollar after direct delivery costs, so the 11.2% electricity and fuel shock was partly offset by the $9.00 price and growing parcel volumes. The 12.0% to 14.0% operating result shows overheads were controlled as the business expanded, and the 18.0% to 21.0% return on capital employed shows existing assets produced more operating profit even while the $560,000 van fleet was being funded. Interest payable remains low relative to operating profit, so the $360,000 loan is manageable. A caution is that capital employed grew quickly, so the new vans must generate enough parcels to maintain these returns.

Conclusion: FLE's financial performance has improved. Gross margin, operating margin and return on capital employed all rose together between 2024 and 2025, showing broad-based progress rather than a one-off gain. FLE should proceed with the van fleet while checking that the new assets earn comparable returns and that the 2.9% mis-sort rate is reduced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three profitability ratios for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of margins, operating profit and capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FLE of offering carbon-neutral delivery for its online-retailer clients.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 400 online retailers found 68% would pay up to $0.30 more for carbon-neutral delivery, so FLE can add a premium that protects its $4.50 contribution per unit while electricity and fuel costs rise 11.2%. It also appeals to the 55% of retailers who rank delivery speed first, since a modern electric fleet supports reliable, fast service and helps win the contracts needed to justify the $560,000 investment.

Disadvantage: Electric vans and carbon-neutral operations require charging infrastructure and may have limited range, which could raise the $180,000 fixed costs and disrupt the 52,000-parcel schedule on longer routes. If vans run out of charge or deliveries slip, the 2.9% mis-sort and late-delivery problem worsens, prompting complaints and possible loss of retailer contracts. The $360,000 loan also leaves little spare cash to fund an expensive green transition if the $0.30 premium is not accepted across all parcels. Range limits on longer routes could also worsen the punctuality that 55% of retailers rank first.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FLE's survey data, costs and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in electricity and fuel input costs will affect FLE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): If FLE's $360,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $360,000 = $2,700 a year (0.0075 × $360,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $180,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may also make retailers cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing, but FLE can largely remove this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 per hour): FLE employs a workforce of 40, with many couriers and depot staff likely paid hourly, so a wage rise feeds into its cost base and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 52,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 1,300 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is affordable; if labour turnover at 14% disrupts the depot, unit labour cost rises and the $4.50 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Electricity and fuel inputs (11.2%): FLE's variable cost of $4.50 per unit will be affected, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.2% it would add 11.2% × $4.50 = $0.50 per unit, and at 52,000 units that is about $26,000 a year (52,000 × $0.50). Even a smaller pass-through cuts the $4.50 contribution materially. FLE can offset some of this through the $0.30 carbon-neutral premium in the survey.

Conclusion: The 11.2% electricity and fuel rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 52,000 parcels and directly erodes the $4.50 contribution that supports the $560,000 fleet. The wage rise is second because it can be managed through productivity; the interest-rate effect is smallest and can be fixed. FLE should secure the $0.30 premium and improve route efficiency to protect margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to FLE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FLE's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of FLE with a well-justified judgment that energy costs have the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
